texts.title: The long goodbye of the cheque

paragraphs.text: A cheque is a letter to a bank, written by a customer, instructing it to pay a named person a stated sum. For most of the twentieth century it was how households and businesses moved money that was too large for cash and too slow for a bank visit, and the volumes were enormous: at their peak in the late 1980s, several European countries were clearing billions of cheques a year, and the paper was physically flown between cities overnight. Almost every part of that arrangement has now gone, and the way it went is more interesting than the fact that it did. An instrument that everyone used and nobody now misses is a good place to watch how a habit is actually replaced.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Cheques declined because they were expensive to handle, not because customers disliked them. Every cheque had to be read, sorted, transported and matched against an account, and although machines could read the magnetic characters along the bottom, the handwritten amount usually could not be captured automatically. Banks were therefore paying for clerks, vans and aircraft to move paper whose value could be transmitted electronically for a fraction of the cost. The pressure to replace the instrument came from the industry, and the industry was careful about how it applied that pressure. Charging customers directly for each cheque would have been simpler and was avoided in most markets, because the cost of the resulting argument was judged to exceed the saving.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The first replacement was not a card but a standing instruction. Recurring payments, which are the bulk of household outgoings, moved to direct transfers between accounts on a fixed date, and the change was largely invisible to the payer. Card payments then absorbed the retail end, and mobile transfers took the person-to-person payments that cash and cheques had shared. By the time anyone noticed that the chequebook had not been opened in a year, the instrument had lost three of the four things it was used for. None of those three replacements was sold as a way of killing the cheque; each was sold as a convenience, and the effect was the same.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: What remained was the awkward fourth. A cheque can be handed to someone whose bank details you do not know, it can be posted with a letter, it can be written by a person with no telephone and no computer, and it leaves a record that both sides hold. Those properties matter for a small number of transactions and for a number of people that is small in percentage terms and large in absolute terms: the very old, the rural, and organisations such as clubs and charities whose treasurer changes every year.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Attempts to end the instrument by decree have usually been withdrawn. One banking industry announced a date after which cheques would not be accepted, discovered that no acceptable alternative existed for several of the uses above, and cancelled the plan after public objection. The lesson learned in several countries was that an instrument disappears when its last use has a better substitute, and not before; setting a date for the disappearance does not create the substitute. Regulators in several places now require banks to keep accepting cheques until a named alternative exists for each remaining use.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The technical response was to keep the instrument and remove the paper journey. Under imaging systems now used in a number of countries, a cheque is photographed at the point of deposit — often by the customer with a phone — and the image, rather than the paper, is sent for clearing. Settlement fell from several working days to one or two, fraud has not risen in the way that was predicted, and the cost of handling has dropped enough that the remaining volumes are no longer an argument for abolition.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The story has a wider moral about legacy systems. A technology that is obsolete in nine uses out of ten is not obsolete at all if the tenth has no replacement, and the cost of maintaining it falls on the institution while the benefit of retiring it is diffuse. The cheapest resolution is usually the one that was reached here: keep the interface that people understand, replace the machinery behind it, and let the volumes fall on their own. The instrument that survives that treatment is usually a different thing wearing the same name.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Almost every plant in a forest is connected to fungi. The threads of a fungus wrap around or penetrate the fine roots of a tree, and the two exchange goods: the tree supplies sugars made in its leaves, the fungus supplies water and mineral nutrients gathered from a volume of soil that roots alone could never reach. The arrangement is ancient, it is found in the great majority of land plants, and it was described in detail more than a century ago. Nothing in that description was controversial until the arrangement was given a nickname and a personality.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: What caught the public imagination was the next step. Because one fungus can be connected to several trees at once, the threads form a network through which material can in principle move from tree to tree. Experiments using carbon labelled with a rare isotope showed that carbon fed to one tree could later be detected in a neighbour, and the finding was reported in terms that suggested trees were deliberately feeding each other, with older trees described as nursing seedlings through the shade. The phrase that stuck, coined by a journalist rather than by the researchers, compared the arrangement to a communication network, and the comparison has been doing the arguing ever since.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The evidence is real and the interpretation was pushed further than it will bear. The transfer is not disputed; what is disputed is how much of it there is, whether it moves through the fungus or through the soil after leaking from roots, and whose interests it serves. A fungus is not a pipe operated by trees for their mutual benefit; it is an organism with its own requirements, and material that passes through it may simply be paying for its own metabolism on the way.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Careful reviews have made three points that are easy to lose. First, most of the field experiments were done on a small number of species in a small number of forests, and the results do not transfer automatically to a plantation, a tropical forest or a hedge. Second, the amount of carbon moved between trees is usually a small fraction of what a seedling needs, which makes the nursing story implausible as a general account. Third, several widely repeated claims can be traced to single studies whose own authors described them as preliminary.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: None of this makes the networks unimportant; it makes them ordinary, which is a different thing. The fungal partners plainly change how a forest works: they determine which nutrients are available to which tree, they alter the outcome of competition between seedlings, and they are the route by which many trees acquire phosphorus and nitrogen. A forest with its fungi removed behaves very differently from one with them, and that is an enormous effect without any need for cooperation between trees. The interesting question is not whether trees help each other but how a partnership between two very different organisms stays stable at all.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The fungi also carry costs. Some of them move carbon in one direction only, taking from a plant that gets nothing in return, and a number of plants have abandoned photosynthesis entirely and live as parasites on the network. Disease can travel through the same threads that carry nutrients. The network is therefore not a benevolent commons but a market with cheats in it, which is the ordinary condition of anything involving more than one species.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The practical questions for forestry are more useful than the poetry. Replanting a clear-felled area with seedlings raised in sterile compost often fails because the fungal partners are missing from the soil and from the roots, and inoculating seedlings before planting improves survival in those conditions. Machinery that compacts the ground damages the fungal network more than it damages the trees. Whether it is worth transplanting soil from an old wood into a new one is being tested, and the early results are mixed. What is not in doubt is that a plantation established without attention to the soil community takes longer to close its canopy than one established with it.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The episode is a useful lesson about how a finding travels. A careful paper reporting measurable transfer between trees became, within a decade, a claim that forests are communicating organisms, and the claim reached the public through books and documentaries before the reviews caught up. Researchers who now publish careful qualifications find themselves described as debunkers of something they never denied, and the correction travels slower than the story did, as corrections generally do.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: How old is old enough to drive?

paragraphs.text: The age at which a person may drive alone varies more than almost any other legal threshold: sixteen in some jurisdictions, eighteen in most of Europe, and twenty-one for certain vehicle classes. The variation is not the result of different evidence, because the evidence is broadly the same everywhere. It is the result of different answers to a question the evidence cannot settle, which is how much risk a society will accept in exchange for the mobility of its young people.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ana Belova works on the crash statistics and considers the pattern beyond argument. Drivers in their first year are involved in collisions at several times the rate of drivers in their fifth, the excess is concentrated in the first six months, and the curve falls with experience rather than with age. Two factors sit behind it: a driver who has not met a situation before responds slowly, and a brain that is still developing discounts risk in the presence of friends more than it does alone. The second factor is why passenger restrictions work.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Piet Kessler is interested in what those numbers leave out. Crash rates are reported per licensed driver or per kilometre, and both denominators hide something: a country that licenses at eighteen has fewer young drivers and a higher rate among those it has, while a country that licenses at sixteen spreads the same learning period over more people. He argues that the honest comparison counts crashes per head of the age group, that on this measure several of the famous international differences shrink, and that the remaining difference is mostly about how much driving young people do at all.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Rosa Iglesias approaches it as a design problem rather than a threshold. Graduated licensing gives a learner a full period of supervised driving, then a restricted licence with limits — no driving late at night, no passengers under a certain age, a lower alcohol limit — and lifts the limits in stages. Jurisdictions that introduced it saw crash rates among the youngest drivers fall by between a fifth and a third, and the effect is largest where the supervised period is long and is enforced. The age of first licence, on her account, matters much less than what happens in the two years after it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Tomasz Wrona raises the cost that is rarely counted. Where public transport is thin, a licence is access to work, to training and to medical appointments, and raising the age transfers that cost onto exactly the households least able to absorb it. Rural young people drive earlier out of necessity and are over-represented in the crash statistics partly for that reason. Any policy that treats the licence as a privilege, he argues, should be accompanied by a transport alternative, and almost none of them are.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What none of them disputes is that the vehicle has changed the arithmetic. Electronic stability control, automatic braking and lane keeping have cut the crash types that inexperience produces most often, and the fall in young driver deaths over three decades owes more to the cars than to the licensing rules. The effect is uneven in a predictable direction: new safety equipment reaches new cars first, and young drivers drive old cars.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Where does that leave a legislator? With a menu rather than a number. Raising the age reduces exposure and shifts the problem a year later; graduated licensing reduces the risk within the exposure; passenger and night restrictions target the specific conditions in which the excess occurs; and investment in the vehicle fleet does more than any of them but is not a licensing policy at all. The evidence ranks these; it does not tell a country which of them it can afford.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The honest summary is that the question is not really about age. Almost every measure that works targets experience, conditions or equipment, and age is a proxy that is easy to legislate and poorly aimed. A country that raises the age and does nothing else has bought a real reduction in crashes and has paid for it in mobility, and whether that is a good trade depends on what its young people would otherwise be able to reach. Nobody who argues about this in public puts it that way, which is part of why the argument has lasted so long and moved so little.
paragraphs.label: H
